segments.text: Mr. Barthelemy called attention to the fact that the second assembly had proposed an amendment to the covenant enabling the assembly to draft a system of rules, that this amendment had not been ratified, and that it was doubtful whether the assembly adopt a system at present; that the committee submitting this amendment to the second assembly had made a reservation safeguarding the liberty of the assembly. To meet the situation, he said, the first committee now functioning had presented: (1) A reso­ REGULATIONS lution containing rules of procedure for the ballot within the assembly; (2) a resolution containing a pronouncement of principle and substance; and (3) a recommendation. He added that the committee took no definite position as t<> the legal force of its declaration and reserved the liberty of follows: the next assembly.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1135
segments.text: Prince Arfa-Ed-Dowleh, Persia, asked that in electing nonpermanent members the assembly should consider the geographical situation, ethnical, religious, and commercial conditions of the various systems of civilization, and that a seat should be allotted to Asia with its 850,000,000 people. Lord Balfour, British Empire, proposed a redraft of the preamble of the second resolution, as follows:

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1136
segments.text: Pending the ratification by the states of the amendment of article 4 of the covenant voted by the assembly in 1921, and without prejudice to the right of the assembly " to · select in its discretion," in accordance with the provisions of the covenant the nonpermanent members of · the council, the assembly recommends the fourth assembly to adopt the following regulations, Lord Balfour explained that this redraft would mean the elision of the eighth paragraph of the second resolution; that in this way unanimity would be obtained in the assembly; that it was desirable, however, to recommend to states members ratification of amendments to the covenant proposed by the second assembly so that the fourth assembly might not find itself in position similar to that now facing the third.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1137
segments.text: Mr. Bourgeois, France, supported the proposal of Balfour. The president announced a motion by Lord Balfour in the following terms:

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1138
segments.text: The assembly declares that it is of the highest importance that the amendments to the covenant already passed should be ratified by the governments of the members of the league, and requests the council to take all proper measures to secure this result.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1139
segments.text: Mr. Scialoja, Italy, approved the Balfour motion and suggested that if the assembly desired to recommend ratification it should consider the text of a recommendation drafted by the first committee in this language:

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1140
segments.text: The assembly calls the attention of the delegations to the fact that it is of the utmost importance for the authority and the proper working of the League of Nations that the states should ratify at a very early date the amendments of the covenant voted by the first and second assemblies, with the exception of amendments 2 and 3 to article 6. •

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1141
segments.text: He added that the first committee recommended immediate ratification of the first amendment to article 6, so that the assembly could fix rules for election of members of council.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1142
segments.text: Mr. Tang-Tsai Fow, China, thanked the Persian delegate for the testimony he had borne to the solidarity of Asia, and referred to the action of China in submitting to the first committee draft regulations for election of nonpermanent members of council on the principle of geographical distribution, five seats to go to European and American members, the sixth to a non-European and non-1\merican state. He contended that this would have assured the universal character of the council, awakening interest of countries remote from the sphere of the activities of the league, and facilitating rotation by giving every member a chance to sit on the council. He pointed out that the first assembly had made formal recommendations to this effect. He added that the first committee, however, had deemed it in line with duty to adopt a compromise between two points of view and that the Chinese delegation, in a spirit of conciliation, reserving future liberty, would support the committee action.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1143
segments.text: Lord Balfour announced his acceptance of Mr. Scialoja's suggestion.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1144
segments.text: Mr. Motta, Switzerland, announced his approval of the Balfour proposals with the understanding that they did not affect the substance of the resolutions.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1145
segments.text: Resolutions as amended and recommendation carried.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1146
segments.text: Lord Balfour's motion regarding ratification, as amended, was then adopted.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1147
segments.text: Twenty-third meeting, Friday, September 29, 1922, 3.30 p. m.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1148
segments.text: FOR FINANCIAL ADMINISTRATION OF LEAGUE-FOURTH COMMITTEE REPORT

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1149
segments.text: Mr. Zahle, Denmark, president, Mr. Melot, Belgium, reporter, fourth committee, took seats on platform, Mr. Melot presenting report and conclusions, the latter being as Whereas the recommendation of the assembly adopted on September 17, 1920, with regard to the administration of the finances of the League of Nations, as modified by the recommendations of October 4, 1921, requested the council to prepare for the annual session of the assembly in 1922, a final resolution concerning the administration of the finances of the League of Nations;

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1150
segments.text: And whereas the council requested the commission of control to prepare a draft of such a resolution, and the commission has submitted such a draft which has been considered by the assembly. The assembly of the League of Nations adopts the regulations for the administration of the finances of the League of Nations. Conclusions adopted by assembly.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1151
segments.text: BUDGET AND ACCOUNTS; REPORT BY FOURTH COMMITTEE

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1152
segments.text: Mr. Zahle, Denmark, chairman; Mr. Adatci, Japan, reporter, fourth committee, came to seats on platform, the reporter presenting the following resolution:

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1153
segments.text: The assembly of the League of Nations finally passes the expenditure and income accounts for the third fiscal period ending December 31, 1921.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1154
segments.text: The reporter, Mr. Adatci, stated that the budget estimates for the period 1923 showed an inevitable increase over prior ones, and urged the reduction of expenditures to the minimum. The forthcoming budget, he said, called for 25,623,000 francs, making the unit contribution 27,851 francs. He told the assembly that the fourth assembly had cut down all expenditures not absolutely indispensable.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1155
segments.text: Mr. Rivas-Vicuna, Chile, regretted the existing system which controlled finances in accordance with the requirements of the administration and calculated receipts only afterwards in accordance with its needs; that expenditure should be stabilized, the contribution of each state determined and the budget regulated in consonance with resources available. He urged that the league make sure that the states embodied their contributions in their budgets; that an increase, however, in the league budget, without modifying the number of units, would weigh heavily on states in financial difficulties; that the value of each unit be fixed for three or five years; that the council submit such a plan to the next assembly.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1156
segments.text: Sir James Allen, New Zealand, urged acceptance of scale proposed, and that delegates urge their governments to pay annual contributions as soon as possible. He asserted that the financial position of the league was disquieting, that contributions in arrears amounted to more than 14,000,000 francs, causing a deficit; that the league would be compelled to raise a loan from the banks if amounts due were not paid; that delegates should urge their governments to pay their contributions for 1923 as soon as possible, as well as all or part of arrears.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1157
segments.text: Mr. Urrutia, Colombia, stated that it was difficult to induce parliaments to vote larger sums each year for the league; that he hoped the league budget would not increase during the next few years; and that no new technical bodies would be formed until the league was on a permanent footing.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1158
segments.text: Mr. Amador, Panama, asserted that the increasing league budget and the deficit were disquieting to the parliament of his country; that the true friends of the league would continue to support in every way and that every effort must be made to guard against an excessive increase of expense.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1159
segments.text: The resolution was agreed to.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1160
segments.text: Mr. Adatci then presented a second resolution from the fourth committee, as follows:

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1161
segments.text: The assembly adopts the first report of the commission of control and the supplementary report in so far as its recommendations have not already been acted upon or are not at variance with other specific decisions of the third assembly or of its fourth committee. Resolution agreed to.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1162
segments.text: Mr. Adatci, for the fourth committee, next submitted two additional resolutions in the following terms:

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1163
segments.text: (a) The assembly recommends that, in view of the necessity of realizing economies in the financial administration of the league, the council should always hold its sessions at Geneva except in the case of absolutely exceptional circumstances necessitating a session at some other place.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1164
segments.text: (b) The assembly of the League of Nations, in accordance with article 4 of the recommendations adopted by the first assembly on the administration of the finances of the League of Nations dated September 17, 1920, approves for the fiscal period 1923 the general budget of the league and the budget of the international labor organiz a tion and the supplementary credits, amounting in all to 25,623 , 508 francs, and decides that these budgets shall be published 1n the official journal.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1165
segments.text: Mr. Reynald, France, observed that all members of the assembly favored economy, but that the intellectual organization had been too parsimonious; that the allowed credit of 50,000 francs should be doubled; that the international labor office was worthy of praise, but gave insufficient attention to the organization of intellectual work; that the material welfare of intellectual workers should be looked after and their organization placed on an international basis.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1166
segments.text: The Maharajah of Nawanagar, India, supported Mr. Reynald, contending that nothing was more important than restoration of rights due to intellectual activities; that the league should press to a successful ending the work it had been first to begin.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1167
segments.text: Sir Edgar Walton, South Africa, opposed the suggested increase on the ground of economy, pointing out that 75,010 francs had been provided for intellectual cooperation, with a supplementary credit of 50,000 francs.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1168
segments.text: Mr. Zumeta, Venezuela, argued that a vote for the increase would do honor to the league.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1169
segments.text: Sir Joseph Cook, Australia, deemed the provision already made to be sufficient and opposed the addition from the standpoint of economy.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1170
segments.text: Mr. Fielding, Canada, took the economical view and opposed the suggested increase, claiming also that there had not been sufficient time properly to study the matter.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1171
segments.text: Mr. Bellegarde, Haiti, favored the increase, holding that it was too small to render the financial situation more com . ­ plicated.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1172
segments.text: Mr. Adatci, reporter, said he was in personal sympathy with the proposal, but asked that it be withdrawn for the coming year in the interest of harmony.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1173
segments.text: Mr. Reynald insisted on his suggestion, which he presented in these terms:

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1174
segments.text: The assembly-

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1175
segments.text: In view of the fact that the work undertaken by the committee on intellectual cooperation, in accordance with the decision of the second assembly, can not be satisfactorily carried out without adequate financial provisions in the budget--

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1176
segments.text: Decides to raise the credits shown for this purpose under the heading of International Bureau and Miscellaneous Questions to the sum of 175,000 francs.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1177
segments.text: Proposal adopted.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1178
segments.text: Committee resolutions as amended by Mr. Reynold's pro· posal were then carried.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1179
segments.text: BUILDING SITES OFFERED BY SWISS CONFEDERATION AND BY CANTON AND CITY OF GENEVA

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1180
segments.text: Mr. Adatci, for fourth committee, submitted the following resolution:

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1181
segments.text: The assembly of the League of Nations, having noted the letter from the Swiss delegation, dated September 14, 1922, addressed to the secretariat of the League of Nations on behalf of the federal council and on behalf of the council of state of the Republic and Canton of Geneva and of the administrative council of the city of Geneva, which provides that, subject to the ratification by the constitutional powers, both Federal and Genevese, and in order to assist the league to acquire 1n due time premises suitable for the holding of the assembly and for use as offices by the International Labor Office, by obtaining possession of land in Geneva suitably placed for their requirements, the following sites are offered as a gift:

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1182
segments.text: (1) On the part of the Swiss Confederat(ion, the premises situated at 154, Rue de Lausanne, on the shores of the lake, and having an area of 35 , 845 square meters;

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1183
segments.text: (2) On the part of the Republic and Canton of Geneva and the city of Geneva, the land adjacent to the secretariat on the side nearest to the city and having an area of 4,493 square meters; expresses its warm appreciation of the generosity and the good will shown toward the League of Nations which inspired these offers and gives full powers to the council:

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1184
segments.text: (1) To accept these offers as soon as they have both been definitely made; and

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1185
segments.text: (2) To authorize the secretary general to act on behalf of the League of Nations to carry out the transfer of the property rights. Resolution adopted and the president authorized to address a letter of thanks to the Swiss authorities.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1186
segments.text: LIMITATION OF COUNCIL EXPENDITURES

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1187
segments.text: Mr. Adatci, from fourth committee, submitted this resolution:

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1188
segments.text: The assembly, considering that the present financial position of all countries renders the strictest economy necessary on the part of the League of Nations, especially in so far as new work involving the league in new expenditure is concerned, even if this work was contemplated by conventions or resolutions antedating the present session of the assembly:

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1189
segments.text: Requests the council of the league and the governing body of the international labor office to see that work of this nature should be undertaken between the third and fourth assemblies only in cases of extreme urgency.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1190
segments.text: The assembly also requests the council of the league and the governing body of the international labor office to submit to the fourth assembly a statement of new work, involving new expenditure on the part of the league , undertaken in accordance with the conditions mentioned in the first paragraph.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1191
segments.text: Resolution agreed to.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1192
segments.text: RECOVERABLE EXPENDITURE

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1193
segments.text: Mr. Adatci, Japan, submitted another resolution from the fourth committee reading as follows:

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1194
segments.text: With regard to the decision of the council dated July 21, 1922, the fourth committee desires to express its full approval of the principle that expenditure incurred for special investigations in the particular interests of one or more members of the league shall be met by that or those members of the league.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1195
segments.text: Resolution carried.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1196
segments.text: DEFERRED PAY AND PENSIONS; PENSION TO DOCTOR PARDO'S CHILD

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1197
segments.text: Mr. Adatci, Japan, brought forward two additional resolutions from the fourth committee which were as follows:

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1198
segments.text: (a) The assembly: .

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1199
segments.text: Whereas, the fourth committee only received the report of the . salaries adjustment committee on the subject of a deferred pay and pensions scheme for the secretariat and international labor office at its last meeting, two days before the close of the assembly; Whereas, it was impossible in these circumstances to consider this question with the necessary care:

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1200
segments.text: Decides to transmit the report that was submitted to it to the commission of control and requests the council to submit to the members a final report four months before · the opening · of the fourth session of the assembly.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1201
segments.text: (b) The assembly feels much sympathy for the case of Doctor Pardo, an official of the international labor office, who died while on a mission to Russia, leaving a young child in difficult circumstances. The assembly duly signifies its approval of the decision of the governing body of the international labor office, recommending that a sum equivalent to one-fourth of Doctor Pardo's salary should be devoted to the maintenance and education of his son.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1202
segments.text: The assembly decides to include for this purpose a sum of donation. '1,500 francs in the supplementary estimates.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1203
segments.text: Mr. Cava~ni,. Italy, observe~ that the scheme devised by the salaries adjustment committee was not acceptable to I the fourth committee; that though the scheme was proposed late m the sessiOn, It might have been possible to have provided a certain payment by employees matched by an equal sum from the league but the committee did not think this

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1204
segments.text: · . t' t t ·t · th 1 ha would be possible; that Great Bn am, never e ~ss, raiSed the question at the first assembly and obtained an approval of the principle; that the second assembly had instructed a committee to devise a plan· that if no account were taken of what the first two assemblies had done a disquieting effect would be produced among the employees; that the third assembly ought to provide a pension scheme for the staff.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1205
segments.text: Mr. Zotlale, Denmark, agreed to the importance of a plan, saying that it meant, however, an expenditure of 750,000 francs a year and a very complicated system; that it had come before the fourth committee too late in the present session; that the assembly should send the report of the salaries adjustment committee to the commission of control and should invite the council to submit to league members a final report four months before the opening of the next assembly.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1206
segments.text: Resolutions adopted.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1207
segments.text: VALIDITY OF VOTE OF INCREASED CREDIT FOR INTELLECTUAL COOPERATION

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1208
segments.text: Mr. Trygger, Sweden, said he questioned the validity of the vote of an increased credit for intellectual cooperation; that in . his · opinion the committee resolution should have been adopted unanimously under the terms of the covenant; that without the desire to raise objections he proposed the submission of the question to the council for examination. The president supported this proposal, holding that it would be helpful to have the council's opinion on procedure to be followed in connection with budgetary questions.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1209
segments.text: Proposal approved by assembly.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1210
segments.text: Report of fourth committee adopted as a whole.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1211
segments.text: AMENDMENT TO ARTICLES 4 AND 7, RULES OF PROCEDURE

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1212
segments.text: Mr. de Palacios, Spain, reporting for first committee, presented the resolution following:

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1213
segments.text: (1) The following text shall be substituted for the original text of article 4, paragraph 1, and paragraph 2 (a) and (b) :

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1214
segments.text: 1. The agenda shall be drawn up by the secretary general with the approval of the president of the council. The complete agenda shall be circulated to members as nearly as possible four months before the date fixed for the opening of the session.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1215
segments.text: 2. The agenda of a general session shall include:

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1216
segments.text: (a) A report on the work of the council since the last session, on the work of the secretariat, and on the measures taken to execute the decisions of the assembly.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1217
segments.text: Subparagraphs (c), (d), (e), (f) shall be, respectively, lettered (2) The following text shall be substituted for the original text of article 7 :

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1218
segments.text: 1. The officers of the assembly shall consist of a president and of six vice presidents, together with the chairmen of the main committees of the assembly, who shall be ex-officio vice presidents of the assembly. These officers shall form the general committee.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1219
segments.text: 2. The president shall be elected at the beginning of each session.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1220
segments.text: 3. Until the election of . the president, the president of the council shall act as president of the assembly.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1221
segments.text: 4. The election of the vice presidents shall take place at one 'of the early meetings of the session.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1222
segments.text: Resolution adopted.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1223

segments.text: PAN AMERICAN CONGRESS

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1230
segments.text: Mr. Van Eysinga, Netherlands, submitted the following resolution, as reporter for second committee:

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1231
segments.text: The assembly expresses a desire that at the next Pan American Congress the members of the League of Nations represented at the congress should call the attention of the latter to the work of the technical organizations of the League of Nations;

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1232
segments.text: Expresses a desire that these members should consider the d means by which any future action contemplated by the Pan American Congress in connection with any question which is being dealt with by the technical organizations of the League of Nations may, a~ far as possible, be carried on in cooperation with these organiZations: and

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1233

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1234

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1235

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1236
segments.text: ALLOCATION OF EXPENSES OF LEAGUE

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1237
segments.text: Mr. de Palacios, Spain, reporting for first committee, submitted a resolution as follows:

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1238
segments.text: The assembly, considering that it is desirable to modify as soon as possible the system of allocation of the expenses of the League of Nations among its members and to replace the scale of the Universal Postal Union now in force by a more just and equitable scale;

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1239
segments.text: And considering that the scale annexed to the present resolution has been recognized by general consent as establishing a more just and equitable system for the allocation of said expenses, and that it is recognized to secure the immediate application of this scale as a provisional measure:

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1240
segments.text: Approves the application of the above-mentioned scale for the allocation of the said expenses for the year 1923.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1241
segments.text: The assembly requests the council to ask the committee for the allocation of expenses, presided over by :Mr. Reveillaud, to continue its researches with a view . to preparing a definitive scale which may be submitted to a subsequent assembly. The assembly leaves it to the council to modify the composition of the committee as it thinks desirable.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1242
segments.text: It begs the council to notify the members of the League of Nations that it is no longer to continue the ratification of the amendments No. 2 and No. 3 of article 6, voted by the assembly of 1921, but on the . other hand to urge them to ratify the first amendment as soon as possible.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1243
segments.text: SCALE FOR ALLOCATION OF EXPENSES FOR 1923 UNDER ABOVE RESOLUTION

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1244
segments.text: Albania, 1 unit; Argentina (subject to observation by Argentine Government), , 35 units; Australia, 26; Austria, 1; Belgium, 15; Bolivia, 5; Brazil, 35; British Empire, 95; Bulgaria, 7; Canada, 35; Chile, 15; China, 65; Colombia, 7; Costa Rica, 1; Cuba, 9; Czechoslovakia, 35; Denmark, 12: Estonia, 3; Finland, 10; France, 78; Greece, 10; Guatemala, 1; Haiti, 2; Honduras, 1; Hungary, 4; India, 65, Italy, 61; Jjiopan, 73; Latvia, 3; Liberia, 1; Lithuania, 4; Luxemburg, 1; Netherlands, 20; New Zealand, 10; Nicaragua, 1; Norway, 11; Panama, 1; Paraguay, 1; Persia, 6; Peru, 10; Poland, 25; Portugal, 10; Rumania, 31; Salvador, 1; SerbCroat-Slovene State, 26; Siam, 10; South Africa, 15; Spain, 40; Sweden, 18; Switzerland, 15; Uruguay, 7; Venezuela, 5. He proposed, he continued, to strengthen the resolution by offering · as a substitute for the words "Considering that it is desirable," the words "Considering that the financial requirements of the League of Nations render it imperatively necessary," and so forth.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1245
segments.text: Mr. de Torriente, Cuba, announced that he would not vote; because his government had instructed him not to accept this year an increase in Cuba's contribution, but that he would ask his government to reconsider this action i! possible.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1247
segments.text: ELECTION OF NONPERMANENT MEMBERS OF COUNCIL

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1248
segments.text: Under rules of procedure adopted at a previous meeting the assembly proceeded to elect the nonpermanent members of the council.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1249
segments.text: The president appointed Prince Arfa-Ed-Dowleh, Persia; Doctor Pusta, Estonia; and Mr. Urrutea, Colombia, to act as tellers.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1250
segments.text: The vote was taken by roll call and secret ballot, and the secretary general proceeded to count the votes.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1251
segments.text: The president announced the result as follows:

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1252
segments.text: States voting: Albania, Australia, Austria, Belgium, Brazil, British Empire, Bulgaria, Canada, Chile, China, Colombia, Costa Rica, Cuba, Czechoslovakia, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, France, Greece, Guatemala, Haiti, Hungary, India, Italy, Japan, Latvia, Liberia, Lithuania, Luxemburg, Netherlands, New Zealand, Norway, Panama, Paraguay, Persia, Poland, Portugal, Rumania, Serb-CroatSlovene State, Siam, South Africa, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, Uruguay, and Venezuela.

The president announced that Brazil, Spain, Uruguay, Belgium, Sweden, and China, having obtained an absolute majority of votes required, had been elected nonpermanent members of the council.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1257
segments.text: Twenty-fifth meeting, Saturday, September 30, 1922, 3 p. m.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1258
segments.text: FINANCIAL REHABILITATION OF AUSTRIA-STATEMENT BY LORD BALFOUR ON BEHALF OF COUNCIL

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1259
segments.text: The president announced that the council, which had been studying the Austrian question during the last few days, desire to report to the assembly on this subject through its reporter, Lord Balfour, and that, after Lord Balfour's address, the Austrian delegate would be requested to speak.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1260
segments.text: Lord Balfour said the Austrian problem had not been entirely solved, but much was being accomplished; that the present was not the first effort the league had made at the invitation of the powers to assist Austria; that the essential part of the first scheme wa,s the release of liens held by a large number of nations, and these were so slowly released that when the last was lifted it was too late, the economic condition of Austria having sunk so low that when the league was asked a second time to intervene, the task was inevitably harder and more complicated.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1261
segments.text: He asserted that if Austria was to secure the needed credit, other nations must guarantee it; that the council and subcommittee of the council on Austria were agreed on that; that four nations had each agreed to take 20 per cent of the total loan required to enable Austria to pay her way during the two years which the council's financial advisers held must elapse before she could balance her budget, the total amount needed being something over 500,000,000 gold crowns; that he had great hope that nations could be found to take the 20 per cent still unsubscribed; that the method in view was the supply of the money by individual lenders, the subscribing nations guaranteeing payment.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1262
segments.text: He then explained that internal reforms must be brought about if the loans were to be had; that large sums had been contributed to Austria during the last two disastrous years, but they had under the existing system no more than sufficed to enable Austria to get along, somehow or another from day to day; that these contributions did not contain i~ themselves a single element of permanence and helped in no way to build a permanent credit basis for Austria.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1263
segments.text: Mr. Pouilly-Dietricbstein, Austria, expressed the gratitude of Austria to the league, and . especially to the members of be 1ts goal. the council, for having undertaken this task, which he sincerely trusted would be successful. He also thanked the nations which had already agreed to guarantee the greater part of the proposed loan, naming Belgium as one of the additional nations which he had learned would take the remainder of the loan, and thanking her also. He said he had hoped the transaction could have been completed while the assembly was in session, but this was not practicable. Lord Cecil asked, that if the project failed would there be a full, public statement of all the negotiations. Lord Balfour said he could not believe failure possible, but, if it came, all the documents and facts would be made public; that the present plan consisted in the main of providing the guaranteed loan; of seeing that it was properly expended in Austria and in cooperation with the Austrian Government; of insuring that it should only be expended in Austria if, accompanying the expenditure, those great reforms were carried into effect, which were absolutely necessary to Austria's recovery; that Austrian sovereignty was to be in no way impaired; that when the plan was completed all the documents connected with the negotiations and the entire transaction would be laid before a public meeting of the council; that with the plan in operation there was no reason why Austria should not recover; that the benefits of the plan would reach Europe and the world, and its success would be an answer to the charge that the league could not deal with the economic affairs of the world; that there was not the least desire or intention of keeping back from the league or the public all the details and all the data on which the council's work in the Austrian matter Mr. Bourgeois, France, said that the council in dealing with the Austrian question had applied the highest and best principles, principles underlying the league, and asked that the meeting end with a demonstration of confidence and faith. He was greeted with loud and prolonged applause.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1264
segments.text: In. closing this, the last meeting of the third assembly, the president, Mr: Edwards, said, among other things, that he thanked Switzerland not only for what she had done for the league but for the living example she offered to the world of a close union which could be attained by a common ideal, even though there was no community of race of religion, or of language. He thanked both Switzerland and Geneva for hospitalities extended. He said that the league was growing day by day, obtaining increased prestige and influence, and winning the confidence of the peoples; that in the first year of its existence the league was composed only of the countries which had been Allies or neutrals in the Great War; that now there were but two of the former enemies of the Allies that had not asked for admission; that every country that had wished to join was now a member· that the doctrine proclaimed by the Argentine Republic at the first assembly, the doctrine of the universality of the league, was being consecrated by the facts that, on account of the close fraternal relations between his country and Argentina, he witnessed with satisfaction the virtual triumph of the Argentine doctrine that would mark an epoch in the history and development of the league.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1265
segments.text: He pointed out that the third assembly had developed the master thought of the covenant, which sought the peace of nations by every possible avenue, by offering to states the procedure of conciliation, a new mechanism, suggested by the Scandinavian nations, impregnated with the basic idea that the league is not a superstate but a center where all the good will alld the peaceful desires of all nations can converge and meet. He referred to the admission of Hungary to the league as one of the happy events of - the third assembly.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1266
segments.text: He concluded with these words:

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1267
segments.text: Ladies and gentlemen, we have reached the third milestone in the journey of our institution. We have nothing with which to reproach ourselves, much to be proud of, and still more to expect. Let us have faith in the destinies of the league, because all that is great, all that seeks the good of mankind and tends toward perfection is imperishable. The origin of humanity is divine, and its end m the beyond is divine also. Perfection, therefore, must When the whirlwind has passed-the hate-laden cyclone loosed over the world by the breath of the Great War-then will the aims and the mechanism of the covenant be more clearly perceived and the serene and limpid atmosphere in which the league has its being become more apparent. We shall see, too, the souls of an the nations of the earth inspired with the ideal of cooperation, yearning to be immortalized, like the souls of individuals-in faith, hope, and charity.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (2), ¶ 1268
segments.text: In another moment we shall have left this hall, and the charge with which you have honored me by electing me as your president will have come to an end. I can not depart without assuring you that to the gratitude which I feel for the great trust you have reposed in me is now added a strong sense of obligation for your indulgence. I beg you to pardon, ladies and gentlemen, the errors I may have committed in consideration of my great willingness for help. to serve you and my not less great desire to continue serving you wherever and whenever occasion may arise. I cease now to be your president, but all my life I wish to be your friend. [Loud and prolonged applause, the whole assembly rising to its feet.]

segments.text: Mr. TYDINGS. Are there any other Senators who wish ask me a question in which they can indicate their readiness to vote now, without further debate?

segments.text: Mr. BARBOUR. Mr. President, will the Senator yield? Mr. TYDINGS. I yield. Mr. BARBOUR. I am ready and anxious to vote now. Mr. TYDINGS. I yield only for a question. Mr. DAVIS and Mr. KEAN addressed the Chair. The PRESIDENT pro tempore. Does the Senator from question? Maryland yield; and if so, to whom? Mr. TYDINGS. segments.text: Mr. DAVIS. Mr. President, why can we not vote now?

segments.text: Mr. TYDINGS. I yield only for a question.

segments.text: Mr. TYDINGS. Yes; I yield.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 89
segments.text: Mr. KEAN. I am ready to stay here not only to-night but every night this week to get an opportunity to vote " yea " on the pending motion.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 90
segments.text: Mr. TYDINGS. I take it for granted that if we were to call the entire roll, there would not be eight Senators in the Chamber who are not ready to vote now. I think it is a shame that the Senate has to be indicted and criticized as a body, and that the responsibility can not be fixed upon the six or eight men who are ready to filibuster on this proposition at a time like this. I am satisfied that the indictment and the criticism which will flow from this day's proceedings, and which will encompass every one of us, as a matter of fact justly ought to be applied to a very, very few Senators.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 91
segments.text: Mr. WALCOTT. Mr. President--

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 92
segments.text: The PRESIDENT pro tempore. Does the Senator from Maryland yield to the Senator from Connecticut?

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 93
segments.text: Mr. TYDINGS. I yield to the Senator for a question.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 94
segments.text: Mr. WALCOTT. I am ready and eager to vote, and vote in the affirmative. It seems to me an outrage that this filibuster is allowed to go on. If it does go on, I am in favor of going on night and day until those engaged in the filibuster are tired out.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 95
segments.text: Mr. TYDINGS. Mr. President, if I thought there was the slightest chance of this measure being enacted, I would not make the motion which I am about to make; btit every Senator in this body knows that it is doubtful if the joint resolution can pass here. He further knows that in the public press the leading member of another body is reported as saying that the joint resolution can not pass the House; that it will not even be submitted to the House in its · present form. Why we want to consider something that there is not the slightest chance of passing, with only 14¥2 days left, is absolutely beyond me.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 96
segments.text: I wish it were possible that a roll call could be had to find those who want to filibuster on this matter, who want to deny to the American people a vote, not on whether they will be wet or dry but on the form of government and constitution under which they shall live. That is all that is involved here-the right of the people to pass upon their form of government-and yet, with all our boasted democracy, we are afraid to let the people pass upon their form of government. They can reject the amendment if the joint resolution is passed, or they can adopt it.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 97
segments.text: Mr. COUZENS. Mr. President--

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 98
segments.text: The PRESIDENT pro tempore. Does the Senator from Maryland yield to the Senator from Michigan?

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 99
segments.text: Mr. TYDINGS. I yield for a question.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 100
segments.text: Mr. COUZENS. Will not the Senator move to suspend the rules, so that we can limit debate?

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 101
segments.text: Mr. TYDINGS. I should be glad to do that; but as I have looked into the matter, with the parliamentary situation as it is at present, as long as this motion is pending there is no way in which we can have a proposition considered to suspend the rules. I thought of that, and submitted it to the Parliamentarian, and he tells me that that would not now be in order.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 102
segments.text: Mr. President, on behalf of those who favor submitting this amendment to the people, I want · to say that a vote to lay this motion upon the table does not mean that we are opposed to submitting this so-called repeal OT modification, in whatever form it may pass, to the legislatures or conventions of the States. It simply means that knowing that it can not be adopted, with only 14¥2 days left, it should be laid aside in order to do at least whatever little bit we can toward bettering conditions in America.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 103
segments.text: Mr. REED. Mr. President, will the Senator permit a

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 104
segments.text: Mr. TYDINGS. I yield to the Senator from Pennsyl­

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 105
segments.text: Mr. REED. Since we have all, or most of us, promised our constituents that we will favor a submission of this question to them, what will they think of our sincerity if, after five hours and a half of filibuster, we cave in without making any effort to break that filibuster?

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 106
segments.text: Mr. TYDINGS. The Senator's question is a very pertinent one; and I am sure that many of us may be misunderstood. However, I pointed put in my first statement that as soon as the Senator from Texas completes his speech, which I understand is to go on for three or four more hours, the Senator from Iowa [Mr. BROOKHART] is to try to get the floor and speak for four or five more hours; and it was only because I realized that perhaps two or three days of valuable time would be consumed, which we could employ to better use in other fields, that I reluctantly have made this motion, realizing that there is no way to break this filibuster except by laying the motion on the table and devoting our attention to other things.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 107
segments.text: Therefore, Mr. President, I move-not that we who will vote for the motion are opposed to the general philosophy of this joint resolution, but because it is the only way in which we can make the most of the 14% days which yet remain-! move, sir, that the motion of the Senator from Wisconsin [Mr. BLAINE] be laid upon the table.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 110

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 111

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 112
segments.text: Mr. ROBINSON of Arkansas. Mr. President, it is well known that at this stage of the session it is a physical and moral impossibility to pass measures which are filibustered against by an organization in the Senate.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 113
segments.text: This motion, however, was made by the Senator from Wisconsin [Mr. BLAINE]. He recognizes the difficulties that inhere in the situation. I am advised that he is not disposed to hold this motion before the Senate to the exclusion of other business. I think, however, that he has not had a fair opportunity to determine whether there is, or will be, a persistent, organized filibuster against his motion, and I think he is entitled to some additional time for the consideration of his motion.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 114
segments.text: Mr. President, this is a pitiable spectacle. It repeats what happened here just a few weeks ago, when with substantially little opposition to a bill, . when the opposition consisted of just a few Senators, we were kept in session indefinitely in order to dispose of the Glass banking bill.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 115
segments.text: I wish to know now whether immediately upon the demonstration of a disposition to filibuster the Senate is going to surrender its right and its opportunity to legislate. If so, I point out to Senators that every bill that is coming on following this motion is liable to encounter the same conditions that are presented here.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 116
segments.text: One Senator has spoken against the motion of the Senator from Wisconsin. I know that the Senator from Wisconsin does not wish to obstruct legislation. I have talked with him about the matter. I feel that the action of the Senator from Texas in yielding the floor to the Senator from Maryland in order to make a motion to table this motion is in a measure an unfair prejudgment of the attitude of the Senate on this question.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 117
segments.text: For my part, I recognize, as suggested by the Senator from Maryland, that if there is a persistent filibuster conducted by a number of Senators, it would be impossible to have a vote on this motion and a · vote on this joint resolution providing for submitting a resolution of repeal; but I do not believe that the matter ought to be concluded until it has been developed that there is a determination to prevent a vote, and I do not think that the display of the attitude of one Senator is sufficient to justify this body in reaching that conclusion.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 118
segments.text: For that reason I shall vote against the motion of the Senator from Maryland.

segments.text: We , the undersigned Senators, hereby move to bring to a close the debate on the motion of the Senator from Wisconsin [Mr. BLAINE] that the Senate proceed to the consideration of the joint resolution (S. J. Res. 211) proposing an amendment to the Constitution of the United States:

segments.text: HAMILTON F. :Jti:AN. RoBERT F. WAGNER. JAMES F. BYRNES. JOHN J. BLAINE. BENNETT C. CLARK. FREDERICK HALE.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 186
segments.text: Mr. SHEPPARD resumed his speech. After having spoken for some time-

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 187
segments.text: Mr. MOSES. Mr. President-

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 188
segments.text: The PRESIDING OFFICER (Mr. McGILL in the chair). Does the Senator from Texas yield to the Senator from New Hampshire? ·

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 189
segments.text: Mr. SHEPPARD. I yield for a question, Mr. President.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 190
segments.text: Mr. MOSES. I am sorry to have missed any portion of the Senator's discussion; but I ask him if, in the progress of his study of the matter of the minorities, he has at all given attention in what he has said to the Senate this afternoon to the question of the minorities involved in that portion of central Europe which is concerned with Rumania and Hungary, let us say; that is to say, the Banat and Transylvania; and, if the Senator has attempted at all to criticize the action of the council of Versailles in the decisions which they made with reference to the minority peoples?

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 191
segments.text: Mr. SHEPPARD. No; I have made no exhaustive study along that line. I should like to have the Senator's opinion regarding it.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 192
segments.text: Mr. MOSES. I am sorry that the Senator has not spent the wealth of his research and scholarship upon this question, because, if he will know, there is still existing a most acute problem, so far especially as Hungary is concerned, with reference to those territories which were taken into Rumania, let us say., wherein, for example, there were to be found-is the Senator yielding the floor?

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 193
segments.text: Mr. SHEPPARD. Not at all.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 194
segments.text: Mr. MOSES. The Senator sat down and I wondered if he was yielding the floor-wherein, for example, there were found those acute questions which grew out of the treaty of Versailles with reference to the consideration of the interests and the rights of the minorities-linguistic, racial, and religious.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 195
segments.text: If the Senator will recall, there were certain provisions in the treaty of Versailles which undertook to set up certain commissions-international in their character, but, after all, American in their results, because the American member happened to be the umpire in each case-to determine the rights of these linguistic, racial, and religious minorities which were set up, and particularly in the section of the globe to which the Senator at this minute has been directing his attention; that is to say, in Central Europe, where in Transylvania, where in the Banat, where in all the interests of Hungary, let us say, without going beyond the confines of any other country, there arose these acute situations.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 196
segments.text: The Senator, having been here, will remember that I happened to be one of that small group who resisted the ratification of the treaty of Versailles, not with reference at all to the 26 articles which made up the Covenant of the League of Nations, but because of those things in the treaty itself which, as I then foresaw, would produce exactly these international controversies to which the Senator is now paying his attention.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 197
segments.text: The Senator at that time resisted me in what I had to say, in what I thought, in what I foresaw. Now he joins me apparently in demmciation of the injustices which grew out of the treaty; - and I am glad to weicome him now to the small, diminishing, but still resisting group of the irreconcilables. I want to ask him, as he discusses this particular question, Why it is that in the course of what he is having to say regarding these problems of which I have now spoken, which involve the rights and the interests of religions, of races, and of nationalities, he is not willing to point out a remedy?

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 198
segments.text: Inasmuch as the Senator yielded to me only for a question, I now come to the question:

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 199
segments.text: Does the Senator join with me in declaring that the injustices of the treaty of Versailles are of such a character that the Senate of the United States should now denounce them?

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 200
segments.text: Mr. SHEPPARD. Has the Senator concluded?

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 201
segments.text: Mr. MOSES. No; I am waiting for the answer to the question, which may be "yes" or "no.~'

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 202
segments.text: Mr. SHEPPARD. The treaty of Versailles provided the machinery for the settlement of all these questions--

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 203
segments.text: Mr. MOSES. 0 Mr. President-

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 204
segments.text: Mr. SHEPPARD. The Senator asked me a question, and he will no_t permit me to answer it.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 205
segments.text: Mr. MOSES. I pause for a reply.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 206
segments.text: Mr. SHEPPARD. The treaty of Versailles set up machinery for the settlement of all these questions when it created the League of Nations; and I suggest that the Senator join with me in joining the League of Nations, so that we can aid in remedying whatever wrongs exist.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 207
segments.text: Mr. MOSES. Mr. President, if the Senator will permit me, the League of Nations has been adequately described as being an instrumentality for settling small disputes among great nations, and as utterly useless in settling great disputes among any nations. I will join with the Senator if he will join with me in a declaration on the part of the United States Senate that the League of Nations, for example, should now ~ake absolute steps for determining what is going to take place in the Far East; whether we and the League of Nations shall permit the Japanese to go forward in Jehol and Manchukuo, and set up there these wholly irresponsible governments under the regis of the Japanese flag. - Will the Senator join me in making the protest of the United States effective, in connection with the League of Nations, or any other body, . that is to say, to the extent of sending the boys from Texas over there to see to it that the Japanese may not overrun Manchuria?

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 208
segments.text: Mr. SHEPPARD. The Senator has leaped from Rumania to Japan.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 209
segments.text: Mr. MOSES. And I will cover the whole globe, because that is what the Senator has done~ - Mr. SHEPPARD. No; I have confined myself to these minorities, for the present.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 210
segments.text: Mr. MOSES. I beg the Senator's pardon; the Senator began at Saloniki.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 211
segments.text: Mr. SHEPPARD. The Senator is not asking me a question

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 212
segments.text: Mr. MOSES. All right; · I will when I finish.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 213
segments.text: Mr. SHEPPARD. Go ahead.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 214
segments.text: Mr. MOSES. The Senator has leaped from Saloniki into the middle East, and his next step, of course, will be into the Far East, and does he intend to take the United States with him? That is my question.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 215
segments.text: Mr. SHEPPARD. The League of Nations is amply able to settle all those questions.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 216
segments.text: Mr. BARKLEY. Mr. President, will the Senator yield?

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 217
segments.text: Mr. SHEPPARD. Does the Senator want to ask the Senator from New Hampshire a question?

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 218
segments.text: Mr. BARKLEY. I want to ask the Senator from Texas whether the League of Nations has under consideration now the repeal of the eighteenth amendment? [Laughter.]

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 219
segments.text: Mr. SHEPPA-.~D. . The League of Nations?

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 220
segments.text: :Mr. BARKLEY. Yes.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 221
segments.text: Mr. SHEPPARD. The League of Nations has a strong organization for the stuty and control of the liquor traffic; and that organization, I am sure, would be against the repeal of the eighteenth amendment. · Mr. BARKLEY. Has the League of Nations the repeal of the eighteenth amendment under consideration at this time? ·

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 222
segments.text: Mr. SHEPPARD. It has the eighteenth amendment under ' consideration at times, because it has the effects of the liquor traffic in all countries under consideration. · Mr. BARKLEY. When will the League of Nations vote on the repeal of the eighteenth amendment? Will it vote on it as soon as we vote on it?

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 223
segments.text: Mr. MOSES ." Mr. President, will the Senator from Texas yield to me?

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 224
segments.text: Mr. SHEPPARD. No; the Senator may answer in a moment. . _

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 225
segments.text: Mr . TYDINGS. Mr. President, · will the Senator yield?

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 226
segments.text: Mr. SHEPPARD. In just a moment. I hope Senators will not all ask me questions at once.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 227
segments.text: Mr. TYDINGS. I will not; I am going to be fair. Will the Senator yield? . · .

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 228
segments.text: Mr. SHEPPARD. The League of Nations, through one of its organizations, as I have said, has the prohibition question under constant consideration.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 229
segments.text: Now I yield to the Senator from Maryland. .

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 230
segments.text: Mr. TYDINGS. Does not my friend the Senator from Texas know that in that pink cup which I lately deposited hibition. on his desk there is nothing but water, without even the slightest trace of alcohol in it?

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 231
segments.text: Mr. SHEPPARD. I am afraid the Senator put half of one per cent in it. [Laughter.]

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 232
segments.text: Mr. MOSES. Mr. President, in reference to what the Senator from Kentucky has said, if he had been here, and had followed with as close attention as I have---

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 233
segments.text: 1\lf_r. SHEPPARD. Is the Senator asking me a question?

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 234
segments.text: Mr. MOSES. I am going to.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 235
segments.text: Mr. SHEPPARD. I wish the Senator would, because I want to finish this address by 10 o'clock.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 236
segments.text: Mr. MOSES. Mr. President, if I conclude with a question I am within the rules. If the Senator from Texas wishes to take me off my feet, all right. [Laughter.]

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 237
segments.text: Mr. SHEPPARD. No, Mr. President; I am not trying to take the Senator off his feet.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 238
segments.text: Mr. MOSES. Is the Senator from Texas going to let me ask a question or is he not?

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 239
segments.text: Mr. SHEPPARD. My friend the Senator from New Hampshire knows that I want to be fair with him. He did not seem to be asking a question, and I simply called that to his attention. Now, let him ask me a question.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 240
segments.text: Mr. MOSES. All right; I thank the Senator very much. The Senator from Kentucky made a reference with re gard to the pendency of the question. If the Senator from Kentucky had been here as continuously as I have, either in the chair or on the floor, and had listened to the argument made by the Senator from Texas, . the Senator from Kentucky would have known that I this afternoon opened my discussion by referring to the intimate relationship of the question before the Senate to the argument which the Senator from Texas was presenting; and, having called attention to that, I now join with the Senator from Kentucky in asking the Senator from Texas just where does he connect any portion of what he has said, aside from that which related to Macedonia, to the question immediately before the Senate?

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 241
segments.text: Mr. SHEPPARD. Through the bureau of the league for the control of the traffic in intoxicating liquors.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 242
segments.text: Mr. MOSES. May I ask another question?

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 243
segments.text: Mr. SHEPPARD. Certainly.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 244
segments.text: Mr. MOSES. Has the United States a representative in that bureau, either as an observer or as a member?

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 245
segments.text: Mr. SHEPPARD. It may have an unofficial observer, because it has been the practice of the Republican adminis­ request. tration to haunt the back door of the league and have unofficial observers present on all occasions.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 246
segments.text: Mr. MOSES. May I ask the Senator another question?

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 247
segments.text: Mr. SHEPPARD. We were a backdoor member of the League of Nations. I know we became so over the Senator's protest.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 248
segments.text: Mr. MOSES. Why does the Senator say "was "? . Does the Senator regard the Republican administration as already in the past tense? . Mr. SHEPPARD. Yes, it is already dead.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 249
segments.text: Mr. MOSES. Without question, that is true, Mr. President, if the Senator will permit me to say so; the Republican Party is no longer in control . of this branch of the Congress or the one at the other end of the Capitol.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 250
segments.text: Mr. SHEPPARD. I thank the Senator for his illuminating contribution to the debate.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 251
segments.text: Mr. MOSES. That . was shown by the vote we had here the other day on the question of going into executive session.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 252
segments.text: Mr. SHEPPARD. I am always glad to have the Senator interrupt.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 253
segments.text: Mr. BARKLEY. Mr. President, I have no desire to delay the Senator from Texas, because . I know how anxious he _ is to draw his remarks to an . immediate conclusion, in which all of us join, I may say; but what I wanted to know was, when will the League of Nations vote on the Blaine resolution?

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 254
segments.text: Mr. SHEPPARD. I can - not give the Senator that information. It will not vote on it but it is interested in pro­

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 255
segments.text: Mr. BYRNES. Mr. President, will the Senator yield to

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 256
segments.text: Mr. SHEPPARD. I yield.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 257
segments.text: Mr. BYRNES. Could the Senator tell us when the United States Senate will vote on the Blaine resolution?

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 258
segments.text: Mr. SHEPPARD. I think it will vote some time tomorrow.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 259
segments.text: Mr. BYRNES. That is comforting.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 260
segments.text: Mr. MOSES. Mr. President, may I ask the Senator another question? .

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 261
segments.text: Mr. SHEPPARD. I will state to the Senator from South Carolina that I am making a connected legitimate speech on an important subject. I have not asked for a quorum call. I have attempted no undue delay, and I intend to finish shortly. To say that one is engaged in a filibuster when he speaks - one day at the beginning of a debate, and does not speak any more, is entirely unjustified, and I do not think the Senator from South Carolina would join any one else in saying I am filibustering.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 262
segments.text: Mr. BYRNES. I simply asked the Senator if he . could give us some indication as to when the United States Senate would vote on the Blaine resolution, and the Senator has said to-morrow. As far as the Senator from Texas is concerned, will he say that he will not seek to prevent a vote on the resolution to-morrow?

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 263
segments.text: Mr. SHEPPARD. I am not seeking to prevent a vote.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 264
segments.text: Mr. BYRNES. And that after this night he will do nothing to prevent a vote?

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 265
segments.text: Mr. SHEPPARD. I am not making an effort now to prevent a vote. I am simply making a speech on a very important subject.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 266
segments.text: Mr. MOSES. Mr. President, I would like to present a unanimous-consent request.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 267
segments.text: Mr. SHEPPARD. I would like to finish now.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 268
segments.text: Mr. MOSES. I ask unanimous consent--

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 269
segments.text: The PRESIDING OFFICER. Does the Senator from Texas yield for that purpose?

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 270
segments.text: Mr. SHEPPARD. No; I do not yield for that purpose.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 271
segments.text: Mr. SHEPPARD resumed his speech. After having spoken for some time-

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 272
segments.text: Mr. LEWIS. Mr. President, may I call the attention of my able and learned friend to the fact that Lord · d Robert Cecil was representing England? It was Smuts who represented South Africa.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 273
segments.text: Mr. SHEPPARD. Lord Cecil represented South Africa by

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 274
segments.text: Mr. LEWIS. That is a matter of which I was not cognizant. I was present at some of the conferences, but was not acquainted with that detail.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 275
segments.text: Mr. TYDINGS. Mr. President, will the · Senator yield to me?

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 276
segments.text: Mr. SHEPPARD. I yield.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 277
segments.text: Mr. TYDINGS. Did I understand the Senator to say that Mr. Smuts was not representing anybody?

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 278
segments.text: Mr. SHEPPARD. ~ He was representing South Africa, too.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 279
segments.text: Mr. TYDINGS. Lord Robert Cecil and Mr. Smuts both were representing South Africa?

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 280
segments.text: Mr. SHEPPARD. That is true, if I am correctly advised.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 281
segments.text: Mr. TYDINGS. That was rather a complete representation.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 282
segments.text: Mr. SHEPPARD. I think so myself.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 283
segments.text: Mr. SHEPPARD continued his speech. After having spoken some time he said:

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 284
segments.text: Mr. President, I ask that the statement under the title "Armenian and Greek Refugees" may be printed in the REcORD without reading.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 285
segments.text: The VICE PRESIDENT. Is there objection?

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 286
segments.text: Mr. MOSES. Mr. President, I would like to ask the Senator to state briefly what is set forth under that heading.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 287
segments.text: Mr. SHEPPARD. Would the Senator like to hear it read?

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 288
segments.text: Mr. MOSES. I would like to have a summary in the Senator's own words.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 289
segments.text: Mr. SHEPPARD. I shall read it for the Senator.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 290
segments.text: Mr. MOSES. If it means what was done by Doctor Nansen and by the League of Nations, association, or whatever they call it, in Athens, which seized the palace of Prince Nicholas and lived in it without rent and tried to charge up the expense to the United States-if that is what the Senator has in mind, I want it read and I want to discuss it with

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 291
segments.text: Mr. SHEPPARD. I shall read it, but the Senator did not ask me a question. ·

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 292
segments.text: Mr. MOSES. Very well. Will the Senator read it and say whether it has to do with what I have just mentioned?

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 293
segments.text: Mr. SHEPPARD. I shall read it.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 294
segments.text: Mr. MOSES. Just a minute. Mr. SHEPPARD. I decline to yield further. Mr. MOSES. May I finish-- Mr. SHEPPARD. I decline to yield further. Mr. MOSES. May I not finish my question? Mr. SHEPPARD. I decline to yield further. Mr. MOSES. I submit to the inevitable. Mr. SHEPPARD. I decline to yield further. The VICE PRESIDENT. The Senator from Texas decline~ to yield further.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 295
segments.text: Mr. SHEPPARD. I shall read it to the Senator.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 296
segments.text: After the conclusion of Mr. SHEPPARD's speech-

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 297
segments.text: Mr. MOSES. Mr. President, will the Senator yield to me for a question?

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 298
segments.text: Mr. SHEPPARD. I yield.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 299
segments.text: Mr. MOSES. The Senator was speaking just now, was he not, of that period when the League of Nations arranged for a loan to Austria, at the tnne when the Abbe Seipel was the Chancellor of Austria? Is not that so?

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 300
segments.text: Mr. SHEPPARD. I take it the Senator is familiar with that matter.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 301
segments.text: Mr. MOSES. The Senator has just been talking about it Mr. McNARY. at length.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 302
segments.text: Mr. SHEPPARD. Yes; but I have not gone completely into the history of Austria.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 303
segments.text: Mr. MOSES. This is not the history of Austria, Mr. President; it is the history of the League of Nations in connection with the Austrian Government, and I am asking the Senator whether he has not been speaking of that period when the League of Nations arranged for a loan to the Austrian Government.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 304
segments.text: Mr. SHEPPARD. It began its arrangements for the loan then; yes.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 305
segments.text: Mr. MOSES. It was about 1923, was it not?

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 306
segments.text: Mr. SHEPPARD. Yes; it began to make the arrangements then.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 307
segments.text: Mr. MOSES. Does the Senator know the history of that loan?

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 308
segments.text: Mr. SHEPPARD. I know something about it.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 309
segments.text: Mr. MOSES. Will the Senator be good - enoUgh to tell the Senate the history of that loan-how much of it was paid, how often the interest was paid, how often they had to readjust it?

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 310
segments.text: Mr. ROBINSON of Arkansas. I object, Mr. President. [Laughter.]

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 311
segments.text: Mr. SHEPPARD. That would require a speech of almost the same length as the one I have made. I respectfully decline to answer to that extent.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 312
segments.text: Mr. MOSES. I am entirely willing to listen. Will the Senator permit still further questions? Does the Senator still yield to me for further questions?

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 313
segments.text: Mr. SHEPPARD. I surrender the floor.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 314
segments.text: Mr. MOSES. I do not want the Senator to surrender the . ' floor. I am seeking information.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 315
segments.text: Mr. McNARY. Mr. President--

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 316
segments.text: The VICE PRESIDENT. The Senator from Oregon is recognized.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 317
segments.text: Mr. McNARY. I ask unanimous consent that the Senate shall vote on the pending motion at 1 o'clock to-morrow afternoon.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 318
segments.text: The VICE PRESIDENT. Is there objection? The Chair hears none, and it is so ordered.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 319
segments.text: Mr. BROOKHART. Mr. President, in view of the agreement to vote at 1 o'clock, it occurs to me that we should modify the agreement previously entered into to meet at 11 o'clock. Some of us want to attend committee meetings in the morning.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 320
segments.text: The VICE PRESIDENT. The unanimous-consent agreement previously entered into is to recess until 11 o'clock to-morrow morning.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 321
segments.text: Mr. BROOKHART. I am wondering if the Senator from Oregon will not agree to modify that agreement?

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 322
segments.text: Mr. McNARY. Mr. President, in view of the fact that we have a unanimous-consent agreement to vote at 1 o'clock to-morrow, and in order to accommodate the Senator from Iowa and others, I ask unanimous consent that the order by which we agreed to meet at 11 o'clock to-morrow morning be vacated, and that when the Senate takes a recess to-night it shall be until 12 o'clock noon to-morrow.

segments.label: Senate, February 14, 1933 (3), ¶ 323
segments.text: The VICE PRESIDENT. Is there objection? The Chair hears none, and it is so ordered.

segments.label: Senate, February 15, 1933 (2), ¶ 67
segments.text: Mr. President, the question before us has had the consideration of the two major political parties. At their national conventions last year they resolved very emphatically upon the question of amending the eighteenth amendment. The Republican Party, referring to an amendment to the eighteenth amendment, resolved:

To effect such repeal we demand that the Congress immediately propose a constitutional amendment to truly representative conventions in the States called to act solely on that proposal.

segments.label: Senate, February 15, 1933 (2), ¶ 71
segments.text: I read these two party declarations for the purpose of calling the attention of the Senate to the fact that both the great political parties resolved for immediate action upon this question. Moreover, Mr. President, I think--
