segments.label: Senate, February 16, 1933 (2), ¶ 249
segments.text: SEc. 3. The sale of distilled spirits for consumption at the place of sale shall not be permitted within the United States or any Territory subject to the jurisdiction thereof.

segments.label: Senate, February 16, 1933 (2), ¶ 250
segments.text: Mr. ROBINSON of Arkansas. Mr. President, the statement just made by the Senator from P~nnsylvania [Mr. REED] is to me astonishing. He proposes to place in the Constitution an inhibition against the establishment of saloons by the States and to justify that action on the ground that the Federal Government shall have no power whatever to enforce the inhibition.

segments.label: Senate, February 16, 1933 (2), ¶ 251
segments.text: Mr. REED. Mr. President, will the Senator yield?

segments.label: Senate, February 16, 1933 (2), ¶ 252
segments.text: Mr. ROBINSON of Arkansas. Certainly. I yield for a question.

segments.label: Senate, February 16, 1933 (2), ¶ 253
segments.text: Mr. REED. I did not say that the Federal Government would not have power. Of course the Federal courts would strike down any State law that established saloons.

segments.label: Senate, February 16, 1933 (2), ¶ 254
segments.text: Mr. ROBINSON of Arkansas. Well, Mr. President, if the Federal Government is to take away from the States the power to regulate the liquor trafflc, in the event it should be legalized under any amendment that may be submitted, it is surprising to me that the Senator should desire to amend the Constitution so as to prohibit the establishment of saloons and also deny to the Federal Government the power to enforce that prohibition.

segments.label: Senate, February 16, 1933 (2), ¶ 255
segments.text: I maintain in all sincerity-and I believe the Senator from Pennsylvania will ag1·ee with me-that if the Constitution prohibits the establishment of saloons that is an implied grant of power to enforce the prohibition, and, if it is not, such a provision is worth less than nothing and ought not to be incorporated in any proposed amendment. -

segments.label: Senate, February 16, 1933 (2), ¶ 256
segments.text: Mr. President, the debate has proceeded to-day on the theory that the States of this Union have few powers and that what powers they have ought to be subtracted from them. It is an astonishing proposition.

segments.label: Senate, February 16, 1933 (2), ¶ 257
segments.text: Mr. SWANSON. Mr. President--

segments.label: Senate, February 16, 1933 (2), ¶ 258
segments.text: The VICE PRESIDENT. Does the Senator from Arkansas yield to the Senator from Virginia?

segments.label: Senate, February 16, 1933 (2), ¶ 259
segments.text: Mr. ROBINSON of Arkansas. I yield to the Senator from Virginia.

segments.label: Senate, February 16, 1933 (2), ¶ 260
segments.text: Mr. SWANSON. Of course, my vote on the various amendments and substitutes will be dependent upon the issues involved. I have a great regard, as have the people of Virginia, for the judgment of my colleague, the junior Senator from Virginia [Mr. GLASs], but as I understand section 2 as adopted last night, it prohibits the transportation and use of any intoxicating liquors in a State, Territory, or possession of the United States that prohibits such transportation and use by its own laws. Is th~t true?

segments.label: Senate, February 16, 1933 (2), ¶ 261
segments.text: Mr. ROBINSON of Arkansas. That is entirely true.

segments.label: Senate, February 16, 1933 (2), ¶ 262
segments.text: Mr. SWANSON. As I understand, if the sale of liquor and saloons were to be prohibited by the State of Virginia or the State of Pennsylvania or any other State in the Union, section 2, as adopted, would allow the Federal Government to prevent the transportation and use of intoxicating liquors within that State. Is that true?

segments.label: Senate, February 16, 1933 (2), ¶ 263
segments.text: Mr. ROBINSON of Arkansas. That is true.

segments.label: Senate, February 16, 1933 (2), ¶ 264
segments.text: Mr. SWANSON. Consequently, it is left entirely to the States to determine in what manner intoxicating liquors shall be sold or used and to what places such liquors may be transported. Is that established definitely under section 2 of the proposed amendment?

segments.label: Senate, February 16, 1933 (2), ¶ 265
segments.text: Mr. ROBINSON of Arkansas. I think that is true.

segments.label: Senate, February 16, 1933 (2), ¶ 266
segments.text: Mr. SWANSON. I should like to ask the Senator-­

segments.label: Senate, February 16, 1933 (2), ¶ 267
segments.text: The VICE PRESIDENT. The Senator from Arkansas has

segments.label: Senate, February 16, 1933 (2), ¶ 268
segments.text: Mr. ROBINSON of Arkansas. Mr. President, I can not yield for other Senators to express their opinions in my time.

segments.label: Senate, February 16, 1933 (2), ¶ 269
segments.text: Mr. SWANSON. I merely asked the Senator if the premises stated by me are correct.

segments.label: Senate, February 16, 1933 (2), ¶ 270
segments.text: Mr. ROBINSON of Arkansas. The language of section 2 is perfectly plain.

segments.label: Senate, February 16, 1933 (2), ¶ 271
segments.text: The transportation or importation into any State, Territory, or possession of the United States for delivery or use therein of intoxicating liquors, in violation of the laws thereof, is hereby prohibited.

segments.label: Senate, February 16, 1933 (2), ¶ 272
segments.text: That leaves to the States the power of regulation; it places the moral force of the Government of the United States behind the States in the enforcement of their laws; and that is exactly what we on this side of the Chamber are committed to, in so far as we can be committed by a platform declaration. Our platform states that we will-

segments.label: Senate, February 16, 1933 (2), ¶ 273
segments.text: Effectively prevent the return of the saloon, and bring the liquor traffic into the open under complete supervision and control by the States.

segments.label: Senate, February 16, 1933 (2), ¶ 274
segments.text: Mr. WATSON. Mr. President, will the Senator yield?

segments.label: Senate, February 16, 1933 (2), ¶ 275
segments.text: Mr. ROBINSON of Arkansas. Yes.

segments.label: Senate, February 16, 1933 (2), ¶ 276
segments.text: Mr. WATSON. The platform of the Senator's party says that" we urge the enactment" by the several States of such laws as will do that.

segments.label: Senate, February 16, 1933 (2), ¶ 277
segments.text: Mr. ROBINSON of Arkansas. The platform reads:

segments.label: Senate, February 16, 1933 (2), ¶ 278
segments.text: As will actually promote temperance, effectively prevent the return of the saloon, and bring the liquor tramc into the open under complete supervision and control by the States.

segments.label: Senate, February 16, 1933 (2), ¶ 279
segments.text: That is what I read.

segments.label: Senate, February 16, 1933 (2), ¶ 280
segments.text: Mr. WATSON. Mr. President--

segments.label: Senate, February 16, 1933 (2), ¶ 281
segments.text: Mr. ROBINSON of Arkansas. I can not yield; the Sen- on ator understands that I have only a few minutes left. I namely, should like to use a part of my own time.

segments.label: Senate, February 16, 1933 (2), ¶ 282
segments.text: The issue here is whether the Federal Government is going went away. to take away from the States all power after repealing the eighteenth amendment, in the event the repeal shall be of ratified. The question is whether we will say, "You must show find some other way of disposing of liquor in the event your pared people are authorized to dispose of it."

segments.label: Senate, February 16, 1933 (2), ¶ 283
segments.text: Now let us look at this question from a practical stand- cation. point.

segments.label: Senate, February 16, 1933 (2), ¶ 284
segments.text: Everybody condemns the saloon. I am no champion of the saloon, and never have been. I have submerged my personal the views, in so far as I am able to do so, and have conformed of them to the platform declarations of my party, believing back"? that it is my duty to take that course. But suppose we say there never shall be a saloon, but there shall be the sale of and liquor. How is it to be accomplished? Is that an implied liquor declaration in favor of the State's going into the liquor York business, in favor of the State's engaging in the sale of liquor? If we deny to the States all power in the deter- never mination of any question as to how liquor shall be disposed that of, what are we going to see done about it? What is the practical effect of it?

segments.label: Senate, February 16, 1933 (2), ¶ 285
segments.text: Granting that the saloon is very unpopular, if liquor is to under be sold at all it must be sold either in saloons or by State officials agencies, and I do not think that the Congress ought to be drinking committed to the policy that we are choosing permanently land, between those agencies.

segments.label: Senate, February 16, 1933 (2), ¶ 286
segments.text: The states of the Union have some measure of responsi- country. bility. They have just as much ability to handle this question as the Congress has, and, from the way we are deal- the ing with it, I am inclined to think just a little more ability tion, than we are displaying. The character of the men who to serve the States in public office is comparable in integrity the and in capacity to that of those who serve the Federal govern Government. This is another illustration of the disposi- in tion of some in public life to take away all powers from the tions States; and I am not willing to do that, particularly in view of the declaration I have read.

segments.label: Senate, February 16, 1933 (2), ¶ 287
segments.text: The statement has been made by the Senator from In- at diana [Mr. RoBINSON] that one who votes for the joint the resolution as it has been amended votes for the return of power saloons. That declaration is not sustained by the facts. States We simply vote, in the event the amendment to the Con- cency stitution is ratified, that the States shall possess some power in determining how this liquor problem shall be handled. soN]

segments.label: Senate, February 16, 1933 (2), ¶ 288
segments.text: I agree with the Senator from Kansas [Mr. CAPPER] that who there is no ideal way of dealing with the liquor problem. the We have been looking for such a way for almost a century, under and it has not been found. Troubles and difficulties inhere and in the problem, and they will not be solved by a declara- knows tion in the Constitution of the United States-which, as drank insisted by the Senator from Pennsylvania, there will be that no power to enforce or carry out-that the States shall not both deal with this subject in accordance with their best judgment. We say that we are opposed to the saloon, and yet over in a time when saloons are unlawful we see them established and maintained in many communities where the law called forbids them; and the question arises, or may arise, in the murders minds of many Senators, as to whether an unlawful speak- pened easy is a preferable institution to a licensed saloon.

segments.label: Senate, February 16, 1933 (2), ¶ 289
segments.text: I do not justify the saloon, and I hope that it may never knows return; and I have grave doubt, in whatever form this New amendment is submitted, whether 36 States of the Union will ratify the amendment. I believe, however, that there is Why sufficient sentiment in the country favoring a change of the facts? present conditions, as they relate to the control of the alcoholic-beverage traffic, to justify this Congress in submitting the question to the people of the United States for whole their decision.

segments.label: Senate, February 16, 1933 (2), ¶ 290
segments.text: The VICE PRESIDENT. The time of the Senator from its Arkansas has expired.

segments.label: Senate, February 16, 1933 (2), ¶ 291
segments.text: Mr. TYDINGS. Mr. President, it seems to me that to a J which great extent we have lost sight here of the real substance of this proposition. One Senator after another has risen this floor and assumed a fact which does not existthat if we repeal the eighteenth amendment liquor is going to come back. I should like to ask when it ever Every man in this Chamber knows that the police records the Capital of the United States-Washington, D. C.­ that in the 10 years following prohibition, as comwith the 10 years preceding prohibition, five times as many persons under 21 years of age were arrested for intoxiTherefore, if five times as many persons under 21 years of age have been arrested in the 10 years following prohibition as were arrested in the 10 years preceding it, in Capital of the United States, right here under the nose Congress, what is the use of talking about liquor " coming Every man here knows that he can go to the telephone have a bootlegger come up to his office and deliver within a half hour. Every man here knows that New and Chicago and every other large city are filled with speakeasies. We know that crime has grown on a scale before seen in the history of any country. We know gunmen have ruled our cities. Yet men have the effrontery, it seems to me, to stand here and say that we are " going back " to this wicked thing called liquor, when the present condition it has corrupted more public and Government officers than ever before, increased among the young, built speakeasies all over the and made hijacking and bootlegging and distilling in an illegal way the words of mouth of every citizen in this I say that we never should have taken this question from states. It is not a national question. It is a local question, it can be solved best in the communities that have deal with it. This Government never was conceived with idea that we would reach out into every community and the habits and the morals and the religion of people those communities. We were to deal with national quesonly-the Army and the Navy, interstate and foreign commerce, post offices and post roads, and the rest of the 18 powers given to us by the Constitution. We bad no right all, except by turning our backs upon the philosophy of

segments.label: Senate, February 16, 1933 (2), ¶ 292
segments.text: Constitution, to go out in the States and assume this and this control. The sooner we give it back to the the sooner we shall establish law and order and deand some respect for government.

segments.label: Senate, February 16, 1933 (2), ¶ 293
segments.text: When my friend the Senator from Indiana [Mr. RoBINgets up and tells about the good women of this land are going to be debauched with liquor he loses sight of fact that the good women of this land are drinking more prohibition than they ever drank under the old regime, every man in this Chamber knows it. The Senator also that more youths are drinking to-day than ever before in the history of this Republic. He knows there is more graft and corruption and hypocrisy in high and low places than ever before happened in this country. He knows that out of 3,000 prohibition agents

segments.label: Senate, February 16, 1933 (2), ¶ 294
segments.text: 25 per cent of them were discharged for discovered corruption in the first eight years of the existence of soprohibition. He knows that there have been more in the city of Chicago in a single year than hapthroughout Great Britain in 10 years of its history. He knows that a criminal ring has dominated that city. He that at this moment there are 5,000 speakeasies in York City, and he knows that bootlegging and illicit distilling go on from one end of this Republic to the other. do we not tell the truth about this subject and face

segments.label: Senate, February 16, 1933 (2), ¶ 295
segments.text: Mr. BROOKHART. Mr. President--

segments.label: Senate, February 16, 1933 (2), ¶ 296
segments.text: Mr. TYDINGS. We have made a dismal failure of the fabric of temperance. We have dragged this country down to a degraded point in its morals, in its temperance, in public behavior, that never existed before in all its annals. Yet we stand here hoping to keep a part of this power has not helped America toward temperance, in my judgment, but has only destroyed the temperance that we have built up through decades of teaching and example and precept.

segments.label: Senate, February 16, 1933 (2), ¶ 297
segments.text: Mr. BROOKHART. Mr. President--

segments.label: Senate, February 16, 1933 (2), ¶ 298
segments.text: The VICE PRESIDENT. Does the Senator fmm Maryland yield to the Senator from Iowa?

segments.label: Senate, February 16, 1933 (2), ¶ 299
segments.text: Mr. TYDINGS. I yield for a question, if it is a brief question.

segments.label: Senate, February 16, 1933 (2), ¶ 300
segments.text: Mr. BROOKHART. Does not the Senator know that when Chicago had 7,000 legally licensed saloons it had 12,000 "blind pigs "?

segments.label: Senate, February 16, 1933 (2), ¶ 301
segments.text: Mr. TYDINGS. I do not yield further. Does not the Senator from Iowa know that right here in the Capital of the Nation, over which Congress has complete jurisdiction, five times as many persons under 21 years of age were arrested during the 10 years following the adoption of national prohibition as were arrested during the 10 years preceding it?

segments.label: Senate, February 16, 1933 (2), ¶ 302
segments.text: Mr. BROOKHART. Mr. President--

segments.label: Senate, February 16, 1933 (2), ¶ 303
segments.text: Mr. TYDINGS. Yes; but that does not count-of course not. The Senator does not want facts. He wants to chase a will-o'-the-wisp, the imaginative prohibition and temperance, instead of the actual thing itself.

segments.label: Senate, February 16, 1933 (2), ¶ 304
segments.text: Mr. BROOKHART. The Senator has asked me a question, and I should like to answer it.

segments.label: Senate, February 16, 1933 (2), ¶ 305
segments.text: Mr. TYDINGS. I have only four minutes left, and I refuse to yield.

segments.label: Senate, February 16, 1933 (2), ¶ 306
segments.text: Mr. President, in my humble judgment, trying to be as fair with all the circumstances as a human being can, I say that I believe that the open saloon was no worse, to say the very least, than the hidden, insidious speakeasy-not a bit in the world-except that we could see the saloon and see its evils; but because we sweep our dirt back of the door, that does not mean that · the dirt has been swept out of the chamber.

segments.label: Senate, February 16, 1933 (2), ¶ 307
segments.text: Prohibition enforcement! Temperance! Morality! Where is it u · under the regis of the eighteenth amendment? What are the gains? Where are they-with the young? With the women? Elimination of the saloon and substitution of the speakeasy? The crime, the murder, the graft, the corruption, the hypocrisy of men who occupy the highest legislative positions in the gift of this Republic? Are there any Senators in this Chamber who have violated the eighteenth amendment or the Volstead Act? Are there any Representatives in the other Chamber who have violated the eighteenth amendment? I do not say there are. Senators themselves know the answer to my question; . and if this law can not be observed in those places, in God's name, where can it be observed?

segments.label: Senate, February 16, 1933 (2), ¶ 308
segments.text: Shall we be a bunch of hyprocrites, lashed by the lash of the Anti-Saloon League, in the face of 13 years of dismal failure; or shall we honestly face these facts as they are now presented, and as every one of us knows them?

segments.label: Senate, February 16, 1933 (2), ¶ 309
segments.text: We have made a failure of this thing. It was doomed to failure from its inception. We ought to be men enough to turn it back to the people of each community, who can settle it better than can we, having in view the conditions in their communities. New York can handle its problems better than the people of Oregon can handle the problems of New York for New Yorkers. Therefore, when we have made the experiment, when we have given it money, governmental support, new courts, new district attorneys, and hordes of agents, and we have failed, in God's name, in the interest of temperance, let us give it back to the States from whence it ought never to have been taken in the first place.

segments.label: Senate, February 16, 1933 (2), ¶ 310
segments.text: Mr. BINGHAM. Mr. President, the remarks made by the senior Senator from Arkansas [Mr. RoBINSON] a few minutes ago show a height of courage seldom seen on the floors of the Houses of Congress. Everyone knows his record. Everyone knows how consistent it has been in this regard. It is very difficult for a public man, it is very difficult for the Congress of the United States to admit that it has ever made a mistake. But we have been trying an experiment for the past few years. Every student of history knew that it would probably fail, because every time in the history of civilized nations a powerful central government has attempted to direct the morals and habits and beliefs or its people, it has failed.

segments.label: Senate, February 16, 1933 (2), ¶ 311
segments.text: When our Government was organized, when the Constitutional Convention was sitting in Philadelphia, the question was brought up as to whether the Congress of the United States should have the right to pass sumptuary legislation, legislation which would deal with the habits of the people, with what they ate, drank, and wore. But these celebrated fathers of the Constitution were keen students of history. They realized that in every great nation in the world when the central government had attempted to control the habits of its people, to make that wrong which custom made right, they failed; that a law could only be enforced when it was actually the crystallization of public opinion. They believed, and correctly, that sumptuary legislation could only be enforced when it was passed by the States or the communities therein, and, therefore, the Congress was not given that power.

segments.label: Senate, February 16, 1933 (2), ¶ 312
segments.text: Beginning about 1812, communities in the United States became alarmed at the growth of drunkenness, at the increase of intoxication, and steps were taken to meet that condition by prohibitory laws in various communities. About the middle of the nineteenth century a wave of prohibition resulted in some 18 States adopting prohibitory laws, but it was found that those laws could not be enforced. When communities containing people whose habits led them to enjoy and not to abuse intoxicating beverages wished to have their manners and customs continue as they had under their fathers and grandfathers for countless generations, they would find some means of accomplishing that result. Therefore, after a few years, nearly all the States, I think with the exception of Kansas and Maine, abandoned the position which they had taken theretofore.

segments.label: Senate, February 16, 1933 (2), ¶ 313
segments.text: Then came another wave of prohibition among the States, and it was tried for a while and abandoned. But in communities which had adopted a " no license " plan by the vote of the people in the community it was difficult, if not impossible, for a socalled blind tiger or speakeasy to exist. Mr. President, in our country, where so many million people are descended from the inhabitants of European nations where for countless generations wine, beer, and other alcoholic beverages have been on the tables every day of the year, it is impossible by any law ~o make those people believe that their ancestors did wrong. It is impossible to make the people of Germany believe that beer is poison when they have seen generations of Germans using it as a daily beverage. It is impossible to make the inhabitants or the descendants of people of Spain, of Italy, Greece, or France believe that wine is a poisonous beverage. When it is abused, it is, indeed, harmful.

segments.label: Senate, February 16, 1933 (2), ¶ 314
segments.text: In adopting the eighteenth amendment, we interfered with the growth of temperance. I know that that statement is directly contraverted by ardent enthusiasts like my friend the junior Senator from Indiana [Mr. RoBINSON], who to-day maintained that a vote in favor of repeal, as we propose to vote to-day, is a vote for the return of the saloon in every State and in every community. That, of course, is a statement not actually founded on what will happen, for there is nothing in what we propose to do that will prevent any State or any community from deciding that it does not want to have alcoholic beverages sold in the community.

segments.label: Senate, February 16, 1933 (2), ¶ 315
segments.text: Where communities consist of people whose ancestors for generations have believed in the temperate use of wine and beer, it is utterly futile for the Federal Government to insist that it knows better, and to undertake to prevent alcoholic beverages from being sold where they are to be consumed. In the News of to-day there is an editorial, very brief, which deserves reading for the benefit of the REcoRD. It is entitled " The Senate's Opportunity " and reads:

segments.label: Senate, February 16, 1933 (2), ¶ 316
segments.text: THE SENATE'S OPPORTUNITY

segments.label: Senate, February 16, 1933 (2), ¶ 317
segments.text: The decision of the voters on November 8 has been put squarely up to the Senate.

segments.label: Senate, February 16, 1933 (2), ¶ 318
segments.text: The Democratic Senate leadership has met the prohibition issue squarely by rewording the Blaine amendment to make it a straight repeal measure, to be passed upon by the voters of the States through conventions.

segments.label: Senate, February 16, 1933 (2), ¶ 319
segments.text: The only proviso ls a restatement of the Webb-Kenyon law, already on the law books, which would write into the Constitution the right of the dry States to have Federal protection against importation of liquor.

segments.label: Senate, February 16, 1933 (2), ¶ 320
segments.text: A vote at 3 o'clock has been ordered.

segments.label: Senate, February 16, 1933 (2), ¶ 321
segments.text: The amendment is the pledge of the victorious party-a party which obtained the largest popular vote in the history of the country, elected a President and Vice President and an unprecedented majority of the Members of Congress.

segments.label: Senate, February 16, 1933 (2), ¶ 322
segments.text: The amendment is an answer to 13 years of foolish attempt to legislate morality by Federal decree.

segments.label: Senate, February 16, 1933 (2), ¶ 323
segments.text: The Senate to-day, by passing this amendment, can put an end to this costly and absurd mistake.

segments.label: Senate, February 16, 1933 (2), ¶ 324
segments.text: We know of nothing that would do more to clear the deck for an intelligent attack upon the desperate economic problem confronting the country.

segments.label: Senate, February 16, 1933 (2), ¶ 325
segments.text: Mr. President, I know that those in favor of repeal are charged by the ardent advocates of prohibition with many crimes, with being interested in promoting the liquor business, with being interested in promoting the return of the saloon, and so forth, ad libitum, ad nauseam. But a study of the figures in regard to intoxication, referred to in part by the Senator from Maryland in his speech a few moments ago, gives clear evidence of the fact that under prohibition temperance has decreased and not increased. Two years ago, from figures which were before the committee, it was shown that there were more people arrested for intoxication in the United States than in the year before prohibition was adopted. Worse than that, far more young people were arrested. Prohibition was adopted to keep the young people from ever knowing the taste of alcoholic beverages. Yet in the city of Cleveland year before last 30,000 persons were arrested for intoxication. The courts in that city keep a record of the ages of persons arrested for intoxication, and we were told by a judge of one of the courts that the average age of those 30,000 persons was only 25 years. In other words, 15,000 of those persons were under 25 years of age, and when prohibition was adopted were not more than 11 or 12 years of age, although it was to keep States. young people from ever knowing the taste of intoxicating beverages.

segments.label: Senate, February 16, 1933 (2), ¶ 326
segments.text: The story is the same all over the country. High-school children who never thought of partaking of alcoholic beverages or spirituous liquors in the days before prohibition now think it is the smart thing to do. There are communities where no high-school society or sorority or other organization can even secure a club or a hotel in which to hold an annual dance because of what goes on.

segments.label: Senate, February 16, 1933 (2), ¶ 327
segments.text: It is because those of us who have studied this question free from bias, and interested only in promoting temperance, have come to the conclusion--

segments.label: Senate, February 16, 1933 (2), ¶ 328
segments.text: The VICE PRESIDENT. The time of the Senator has expired.

segments.label: Senate, February 16, 1933 (2), ¶ 329
segments.text: Mr. BORAH. Mr. President, after listening to the debate to-day, particularly on the subject of the saloon, I have become convinced that there will be no way to prevent the return of the saloon if the eighteenth amendment shall be repealed. I agree with everything the able Senator from Virginia [Mr. GLASS] has said with reference to the saloon, and I am just as much opposed to its return as anyone could possibly be. No power on earth could keep that institution clean, or make it respectable, and I do not want to see it returned. For that reason I am going to vote against the repeal of the eighteenth amendment.

segments.label: Senate, February 16, 1933 (2), ¶ 330
segments.text: Mr. President, what is the situation now? We have in the Constitution the eighteenth amendment, which prohibits the sale of intoxicating liquors, and prohibits their being sold and drunk upon the premises where sold. Gentlemen come to us now and say that we must repeal that amendment because we can not enforce it. Yet they say to us in the next breath, "If you legalize the sale of intoxicating liquors, the National Government can effectively prevent their being drunk on the premises where sold." In other words, we are asked to turn back to the States the power to do everything except control the places where liquor may be consumed. In my opinion, under any possible amendment which can be drawn, that would be a practical impossibility. If we can not prevent liquor being drunk on the premises of 5,000 saloons in New York to-night, when it is illegal to sell it, could we prevent it being drunk upon those premises after it was made legal to sell it?

segments.label: Senate, February 16, 1933 (2), ¶ 331
segments.text: The only way to fight the American saloon is to fight it as it was fought when we adopted the ei g hteenth amendment, that is, to outlaw the liquor traffic and make it an outlaw under the laws of the United States. If we have not the courage to enforce the law against sale, shall we have the courage to enforce the infinitely more difficult task of preventing the place of drinking legally sold liquor?

segments.label: Senate, February 16, 1933 (2), ¶ 332
segments.text: Suppose, as an illustration, there were in the State of New York a system which permitted the sale of nonintoxicating liquors in a saloon, but the Government said that intoxicating liquors should not be sold. Then suppose intoxicating liquors were sold in some saloon. It is proposed to take away the power of the National Government to enter that saloon to see whether or not those in charge were selling intoxicating liquors; to rob the National Government of anY power to supervise the selling of intoxicating liquors.

segments.label: Senate, February 16, 1933 (2), ¶ 333
segments.text: I say that where nonintoxicating liquors are sold-as is now proposed in the beer bill, providing for beer which it is said will be fifteen one-hundreds of 1 per cent of being intoxicating-unless there is a supervising power with full control and authority to prevent the sale of intoxicating liquors, intoxicating liquors will be sold. And even if the power were given, it would be impossible to execute it. Let us not mislead or deceive the men and women who are making the fight against the saloon. If we can not give them real and effective protection, we should not give them a false and ineffective protection.

segments.label: Senate, February 16, 1933 (2), ¶ 334
segments.text: If there is stricken out of this measure the provision for concurrent power, and if there is taken from the National Government any authority or any power to supervise, there will be turned over to the lawless elements of the States the power to do precisely what it is said they are doing now, running saloons in violation of the fundamental laws of the Can we expect the States of the Union which have now repealed all enforcement laws, which have repealed all laws by which to enforce the Constitution, to give us aid in controlling the places where liquor shall be drunk, after we have given authority to sell it and dispose of it? Certainly not. It would be practically an impossible proposition.

segments.label: Senate, February 16, 1933 (2), ¶ 335
segments.text: Mr. Presi~ent, I venture to say here upon the floor of the Senate to-day that, just so surely as the eighteenth amend· ment shall be repealed and the liquor traffic turned back to the States, the saloon as it was known in the old days will return, and that brutal institution, where criminals consort and crime is bred will be running in full blast in less than 60 days after the eighteenth amendment shall have been repealed . . Yea, more than that, it will be running within 30 days after the beer bill, which is now upon the calendar for action, shall have been passed.

segments.label: Senate, February 16, 1933 (2), ¶ 336
segments.text: Governments have tried to deal with the liquor question for a hundred years-yes; for 200 years-yet they have never been able to devise any scheme by which they could control the lawlessness of the liquor traffic. The liquor traffic itself is lawless, and to say that we can control it by permitting liquor to be sold, but providing that it shall not be drunk at this or that particular place, is imposing an impossibility which no governmental agency could execute. Make the sale legal and give the States power and right to set up a system for sale and distribution; make the drinking where sold illegal but give the Government which makes it illegal no power to execute its will or enforce its laws; that is the most consummate legal riddle yet devised by the genius of

segments.label: Senate, February 16, 1933 (2), ¶ 375
segments.text: Resolved by the Senate and House of Representatives of the United States of America in Congress assembled (two-thirds of each House concurring therein), That the following is proposed as an amendment to the Constitution of the United States, which shall be valid to all intents and purposes as part of the Constitution when rati.fied by conventions in three-fourths of the several States:

segments.label: Senate, February 16, 1933 (2), ¶ 376
segments.text: "ARTICLE-

segments.label: Senate, February 16, 1933 (2), ¶ 377
segments.text: " SECTION 1. Article XVIII of the amendments to this Constitution is hereby repealed. The sale of intoxicating liquors within the United States or any territory subject to the jurisdiction thereof for consumption at the place of sale (commonly known as a saloon), and the transportation of intoxicating liquors into any State, Territory, District, or possession of the United States in which the manufacture, sale, and transportation of intoxicating liquors are prohibited by law, are hereby prohibited. The Congress and the several States, Territories. and possessions shall have concurrent power to enforce this article by appropriate legislation. "SEc. 2. This article shall be inoperative unless it shall have been ratified as an amendment to the Constitution by conventions in the several States, as provided in the Constitution, within seven years from the date of the submission hereof to the States by the Congress."

segments.label: Senate, February 16, 1933 (2), ¶ 473
segments.text: Senate Joint Resolution 211, as passed, is as follows:

segments.label: Senate, February 16, 1933 (2), ¶ 474
segments.text: Resolved by the Senate and House of Representatives of the United States of America in Congress assembled (two-thirds of each House concurring therein), That the following " article 1s hereby proposed as an amendment to the Constitution of the United States, which shall be valid to all intents and purposes as part of the Constitution when ratified by conventions in threefourths of the several States:

segments.label: Senate, February 16, 1933 (2), ¶ 475
segments.text: “ARTICLE

segments.label: Senate, February 16, 1933 (2), ¶ 476
segments.text: "SECTION 1. The eighteenth article of amendment to the Constitution of the United States is hereby repealed.

segments.label: Senate, February 16, 1933 (2), ¶ 477
segments.text: " SEc. 2. The transportation or importation into any State, Territory, or possession of the United States for delivery or use therein of intoxicating liquors, in violation of the laws thereof, 1s hereby prohibited.

segments.label: Senate, February 16, 1933 (2), ¶ 478
segments.text: " SEc. 3. This article shall be inoperative unless it shall have been ratified as an amendment to the Constitution by conventions in the several States. as provided in the Constitution. within seven years from the date of the submission hereof to the States by the Congress.”
